content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a conditional image inpainting task guided by panoptic segmentation masks. The proposed model takes in object segmentation information in additional to the image and mask to generate semantically coherent inpaint results. The authors designed an image-level and object-level discriminator to enforce this consistency during training, which leads to better results. Quantitative evaluations show that their model achieves better performances compared to recent models trained under similar guidances.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper proposes to leverage semantic information extracted from segmentation models as a reinforcement for more consistent inpainting images. Corresponding to the extra input information, two specifically designed discriminators are used to enable the generator to learn better and more semantically coherent results within the inpainting mask. The proposed idea is intuitive and effective as demonstrated numerically.

Nevertheless, the proposed idea is quite a naive extension of unconditional image inpainting. It is rather straightforward that with additional panoptic guidance and the respective discriminator during training, the network will produce more semantically consistent results. The introduction of panoptic guidance through a pretrained model however poses an additional constraint, which intrinsically forces the output to have the same object/panoptic labels as the original image, which may not always be desirable. Specifically, what would happen if an entire object is masked, while its panoptic label remains? The authors somewhat addressed this in the unconditional generation section, but could use more extensive explanation for this case. The authors can demonstrate inpaint results after modifying the panoptic mask, which could have larger potential practicality.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is clear and easy to understand. The idea is novel, though relatively naive and simple.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the authors proposed an interesting case for panoptically guided image inpainting. The idea is novel and effective under the constraint but could be extended for a broader use case. The experiments are convincing but call for a minor additional extension on unconditional inpainting.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the study of image inpainting. Due to the lack of semantic information for guiding the broken regions, the output of existing inpainting methods differs greatly from the real images and is prone to structural disorder and other phenomena. For this reason, the authors propose to use the panoptical segmentation information to provide guidance for the inpainting model. In addition, in order to strengthen the guidance of semantic information to the model and improve the credibility of the model output, the authors also propose a semantic discriminator and an object-level discriminator discriminator.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1.	The proposed semantic discriminator helps the model makes up more reasonable content
2.	The proposed object-level discriminators makes the generated content closer to the real images avoiding problems such as disorderly structure of the output content
3.	The proposed approach is easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
1.	On panoptic segmentation guided image inpainting. As the authors state in their paper, there has been previous work using semantic segmentation results to assist the model. Replacing the semantic segmentation result with a panoramic segmentation result and then obtaining a performance improvement is hardly a significant innovation.
2.	The author's presentation is not clear. For example (section 2.1.1 line 7), when introducing the model framework, what  edge map E and  semantic label map L are, there is no correspondence with the Fig 2
In addition, the letter markings of those discriminators in image 2 are a bit too vague.
3.	The results shown by the authors are blurry and hard to see. I wonder what is the resolution of the images used by the authors in the training process. I wonder why all the images in the quality presentation given by the authors are blurry. As far as I know most of the current inpainting methods, the image resolution can be experimentally verified at 256*256 or even higher resolution. Maybe the authors should show the results at higher image resolutions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I don't think the current version of this paper meet the bar of ICLR.
content.summary_of_the_review: While this article achieves some performance gains in image inpainting, the gains achieved are from additional information utilized which may not be obtainable in practise. In addition, the authors are somewhat unclear in the presentation of the method. I think the work in this article needs further polishing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Exiting image inpainting methods cannot well handle the inpainting task with large missing area, where the aritifacts and inconsistencies of the inpainted information lead to low visual quality. Then, the authors propose to solve the problem with panoptical guidence, where supervisons from multiple level are implemented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:

1. Cannot find the edge map E in Fig.2. Moreover, the edge/boudary information already exists in the instance segmentation map, is there any reason to extract the boudary information again and feed it into the generator?

2. Inpainting the large missing area is an ill-posed problem, since most of the missing information can be arbitrary only if it is visually real. Therefore, constraining the output to be a reconstruction of the ground-truth missing area is unreasonable.

3. For the representation extraction of label map L, what is the functionality of the l2-norm? Why is it implemented?

4. Cannot find the difference between Eq.(1) and (2), same with Eq.(3) and (4). For perceptual discrimination, it is conducted on the representation level, which should be showed in the equations.

5. For the perceptual discrimination, the compared representations comes from different encoders/models, which is meaningless.

6. Lacks of the final objective function.

7. Experiments are conducted on single dataset, which is hard to show the capability of the proposed method.

8. Existing work 'Hallucinating visual instances in total absentia. (ECCV2020)', which focuses on object level inpainting should be discussed.

content.title: Panoptically guided Image Inpainting with Image-level and Object-level Semantic Discriminators
content.TL;DR: Guided Image Inpainting and image inpainting with a novel discriminator design.
content.abstract: Recent image inpainting methods have made great progress. However, the existing approaches often struggle to hallucinate realistic object instances in natural scenes. Such a limitation is partially due to the lack of semantic-level constraints inside the hole as well as the lack of a mechanism to enforce the realism of local objects. To tackle the challenging object inpainting task, we propose a new panoptically guided image inpainting task that leverages a panoptic segmentation map to guide the completion of object instances. To enforce the realism of the generated objects, we propose a semantic discriminator that leverages pretrained visual features to improve the generated semantics. Furthermore, we propose object-level discriminators that take aligned instances as input to enforce the realism of individual objects. Experiments on the large-scale Places2 dataset demonstrate the significant improvement by our method on object completion, verified in both quantitative and qualitative evaluation. Furthermore, our framework is flexible and can be generalized to other inpainting tasks including segmentation-guided inpainting, edge-guided inpainting, as well as standard image inpainting without guidance. Consequently, our approach achieves new state-of-the-art performance on the various inpainting tasks and impressive results on object completion.
